This article is an open access article distributed under the terms and conditions of the Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) license ( https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ ). Gaucher disease (GD) is the most frequent sphingolipidosis, caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the GBA1 gene encoding for β-glucocerebrosidase (GCase, E.C. 3.2.1.45). The condition is characterized by hepatosplenomegaly, hematological abnormalities, and bone disease in both non-neuronopathic type 1 (GD1) and neuronopathic type 3 (GD3). Interestingly, GBA1 variants were found to be one of the most important risk factors for the development of Parkinson’s disease (PD) in GD1 patients. We performed a comprehensive study regarding the two most disease-specific biomarkers, glucosylsphingosine (Lyso-Gb1) and α-synuclein for GD and PD, respectively. A total of 65 patients with GD treated with ERT (47 GD1 patients and 18 GD3 patients), 19 GBA1 pathogenic variant carriers (including 10 L444P carriers), and 16 healthy subjects were involved in the study. Lyso-Gb1 was assessed by dried blood spot testing. The level of α-synuclein as an mRNA transcript, total, and oligomer protein concentration were measured with real-time PCR and ELISA, respectively. α-synuclein mRNA level was found significantly elevated in GD3 patients and L444P carriers. GD1 patients, along with GBA1 carriers of an unknown or unconfirmed variant, as well as healthy controls, have the same low level of α-synuclein mRNA. There was no correlation found between the level of α-synuclein mRNA and age in GD patients treated with ERT, whereas there was a positive correlation in L444P carriers. Introduction Gaucher disease (GD) is the most frequent sphingolipidosis, caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the GBA1 gene. More than 400 GBA1 pathogenic variants have been described so far, some of them, such as c.1226A>G (p.Asn409Ser; N370S), c.1448T>C (p.Leu483Pro; L444P), c.84dup, c.115+1G>A (IVS2+1G>A) being responsible for 90% of cases among Ashkenazi Jews population and 60% of non-Ashkenazi patients [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]. GBA1 defects lead to β-glucocerebrosidase (GCase) enzyme deficiency, which results in accumulation of its substrate, glucosylceramide (GlcCer, Gb1), mostly in the monocyte-macrophage system [ 4 ]. The disease course is clinically variable and depends on specific GBA1 variants. Three clinical forms have been identified. The most common form, type 1 (GD1), is believed not to cause neurological damage, whereas neuronopathic forms, type 2 (GD2) and 3 (GD3), are characterized by progressive neurological impairment [ 5 ]. Glucosylsphingosine (Lyso-Gb1) is a deacylated form of glucosylceramide. In GD patients, Lyso-Gb1 plasma concentrations are found to be markedly increased above the cut-off level (12–14 ng/mL), compared to healthy individuals [ 6 ]. The association between patients genotypes and Lyso-Gb1 levels has also been reported. GD patients homozygous for the L444P variant had higher Lyso-Gb1 levels (median, 184.5 ng/mL) than those with the N370S variant on at least one GBA1 allele (median, 143.1 ng/mL) [ 7 ]. Moreover, the brain levels of Lyso-Gb1 were shown to be 22–51 times and 38–694 times higher in patients with GD3 and GD2, respectively, in comparison to healthy individuals. At the same time, the brain levels of Lyso-Gb1 in GD1 patients were found within the normal range and were comparable to those in healthy subjects, thus suggesting that elevated Lyso-Gb1 levels may contribute to the neurological manifestations characteristic of neuronopathic GD [ 8 ]. Therefore, it is not surprising that Lyso-Gb1 is believed to be the most reliable biomarker currently available for the diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment monitoring of GD patients, as reviewed by Revel-Vilk et al. [ 9 ]. Parkinson’s disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder, with an average age of 62 years at diagnosis and a risk of about 3% to 4% in developed countries [ 10 , 11 ]. Aside from the involvement of several commonly known neurotransmitters, including the cholinergic, noradrenergic, and serotonergic pathways [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ], there is growing evidence of the genetic background [ 16 ]. The formation of intracellular deposits of proteins and lipids that precede neuronal damage is believed to be the most critical factor responsible for PD development. The main players in this pathology are the Lewy bodies, with deposits of α-synuclein (α-SNCA), whose robust presence was found in neurodegenerative structures [ 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ]. It is in line with the fact that SNCA pathogenic variants are commonly associated with PD [ 22 ]. Those two discoveries led to the pathological staging of the disease proposed by Braak et al. [ 23 ]. Even now, the fact that α-SNCA deposition occurs early in PD is applied in immunohistochemical tests and is referred to as the gold standard in the neuropathological evaluation of PD [ 24 ]. The α-SNCA protein consists of 140 amino acid residues and reveals a sophisticated nature. Since in aqueous solutions it does not have a defined structure, it was referred to as a “natively unstructured protein” [ 25 ]. However, it has α-helical structures upon binding to negatively charged lipids, such as phospholipids present in the cellular membranes [ 26 ]. Unfolded (native) monomeric α-SNCA is able to aggregate into oligomeric species that can be stabilized by β-sheet-like interactions. Such oligomers can further transform into higher molecular weight, insoluble fibrils, seen in different synucleinopathies [ 27 ]. The association of GBA1 variants with PD and dementia ( GBA1 -associated Parkinson’s disease) has been extensively studied over the past few years. Although GD1 is not associated with neurological impairment, there is an approximately 26-fold higher life-time risk of developing PD compared to the general population. Specifically, from 5% to 7% of GD1 patients may develop PD before the age of 70 and 9 to 12% before the age of 80, with a mean age of 57 years at the onset [ 28 ]. On the contrary, the glucocerobrosidase E326K variant is known to predispose to PD, but does not cause GD [ 29 ]. There is scarce information about GD3 patients and PD, due to the low number of diagnosed cases and reduced life expectancy [ 30 ]. Interestingly, carriers of GBA1 pathogenic variants are also at a higher risk of developing PD [ 5 , 31 , 32 ]. Further studies are aimed at explaining this phenomenon. It was shown that Lyso-Gb1 correlated with elevated α-synuclein levels in neurons from patients with neuronopathic GD or PD and also promoted the formation of α-SNCA oligomers [ 33 , 34 , 35 ]. Although the available data provides some insight regarding the potential roles of Lyso-Gb1 and α-SNCA in the interplay between GD and PD, there are still puzzles missing from the picture. Therefore, we aimed to provide comprehensive data and find possible interactions between GBA1 pathogenic variants, including GD1 and GD3 patients and obligatory carriers from their families, Lyso-Gb1 concentration, and α-SNCA, by considering total protein concentration, oligomer concentration, and SNCA mRNA transcript level.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the molecular relevance of GBA1 pathogenic variants (N370S and L444P) in Gaucher disease (GD) patients (GD1, GD3) on Enzyme Replacement Therapy (ERT), GBA1 carriers, and healthy subjects by analyzing glucosylsphingosine (Lyso-Gb1), α-synuclein mRNA, total protein, and oligomer levels. Key findings included significantly elevated Lyso-Gb1 levels in GD patients and neuronopathic GD, substantially higher α-synuclein mRNA levels in GD3 patients and L444P carriers, but no statistically significant differences in total α-SNCA protein or oligomer levels between groups after multiple comparison adjustment. The research also explored correlations with disease severity, GBA1 variants, aging, and ERT impact, suggesting links to Parkinson's disease risk.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: Gaucher disease patients (65 total: 47 GD1, 18 GD3) were treated with ERT. Doses varied, generally ranging from 15–60 U/kg, with an average of 30 U/kg bm/every other week. While Lyso-Gb1 showed a varied correlation with ERT dosing (the coefficient of determination (R2) for treatment response dropped to 0.16 for high doses >35 U/kg bm/every other week), no consistent dose-response comparisons were reported for all analyzed markers. Blood samples were collected during annual clinical follow-up visits.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: In GD patients, plasma concentrations were markedly increased above the cut-off level (12–14 ng/mL), with all GD patients having levels above this threshold (GD1 median 71.5 ng/mL, GD3 median 64.6 ng/mL; p > 0.05 for GD1 vs GD3). This was significantly higher than GBA1 variant carriers (median 7.51 ng/mL, p < 10^-9) and healthy controls (8.49 ng/mL, p < 10^-8). Elevated levels were observed in one healthy subject and seven GBA1 carriers. GD patients homozygous for L444P had higher levels (median, 184.5 ng/mL) than N370S (median, 143.1 ng/mL). Brain levels were 22–51 times higher in GD3 and 38–694 times higher in GD2 compared to healthy individuals, while GD1 brain levels were within the normal range. The biomarker correlates with disease severity and its correlation with ERT treatment response varied, with R2 dropping to 0.16 for high doses (>35 U/kg bm/every other week). Correlation with age was also reported in supplementary materials.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Deacylated form of glucosylceramide (Gb1) that accumulates due to β-glucocerebrosidase (GCase) enzyme deficiency in Gaucher disease. It is a diagnostic marker for GD, reflects disease severity, and is useful for treatment monitoring. It directly interacts with and stabilizes α-synuclein oligomers in the lysosomal compartment.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Gaucher disease (GD, including GD1, GD2, GD3) patients, GBA1 pathogenic variant carriers (L444P, N370S, and unknown variants), and healthy controls, in the context of Enzyme Replacement Therapy (ERT) and correlation with age.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Most reliable biomarker for GD diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment monitoring. Elevated levels indicate GD presence, reflect disease severity, and may contribute to neuronopathic GD neurological manifestations. It is a potential factor in α-synuclein accumulation and is linked to Parkinson's disease development, correlating with elevated α-synuclein levels in neurons and promoting α-SNCA oligomer formation.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells (PBMCs) lysates, Blood samples

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly elevated and substantially higher in GD3 patients (median 77.48 (2^-ΔcT)) and L444P carriers (median 66.42 (2^-ΔcT)), which was statistically significant compared to other groups. Healthy controls, GD1 patients, and N370S carriers had very low levels (medians 0.83, 0.47, 0.52 (2^-ΔcT)). A positive linear correlation with age was found in L444P carriers (r = 0.74, p = 0.039), while a negative correlation with age was observed for unknown GBA1 variant carriers (decreasing with aging). No correlation with age was found in GD patients treated with ERT (L444P or other GBA1 variant). Correlation with age was also reported in supplementary materials.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Regulates the expression of α-synuclein protein, which is involved in the formation of Lewy bodies and neurodegenerative structures, and is a key factor in Parkinson’s disease pathology. GBA1 pathogenic variants are known risk factors for PD, linking this to neurodegenerative processes.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Gaucher disease (GD1, GD3) patients, GBA1 pathogenic variant carriers (L444P, N370S, and unknown/unconfirmed variants), healthy controls, and in the context of aging and Enzyme Replacement Therapy (ERT) for GD.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Elevated levels, particularly in GD3 patients and L444P carriers, indicate increased α-synuclein expression and may suggest a molecular link to neurodegenerative processes and an increased risk for Parkinson's disease development, given the role of GBA1 variants as risk factors. The positive correlation with age for L444P carriers suggests a specific metabolic link between GD and an increased likelihood of PD for this variant.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Plasma, Blood samples (in this study); also noted in neurons (mouse model) and cerebrospinal fluid (previous study).

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Slightly elevated in healthy controls but not significant; decreased in GD patients; negative correlation with age among GD3 patients.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: The median concentration was highest in the control group (1.34 ng/mL), with GD patients having 0.16 ng/mL and GBA1 carriers 0.54 ng/mL. The difference between GD patients and controls was statistically significant (p = 0.0075) before multiple comparison adjustment but not after. A moderately negative linear correlation with age was found among GD3 patients (r = -0.52, p = 0.029), and levels were observed to decrease with ERT duration (partially supported). Mouse models showed an increase in α-SNCA concentration with GCase deficiency, while a previous study on cerebrospinal fluid revealed decreased α-SNCA levels among GBA1 pathogenic variant carriers. Correlation with age was also reported in supplementary materials.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Plays a role in the etiopathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases, particularly Parkinson's disease. Increased concentration and polymerization can lead to neurotoxicity, and GBA1 pathogenic variants are risk factors for PD.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Gaucher disease (GD) patients, GBA1 variant carriers, GCase deficiency, aging, duration of Enzyme Replacement Therapy (ERT) treatment, and comparison to healthy controls.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A potential indicator of neurotoxicity and risk for Parkinson's disease. Although not statistically significant after adjustment, lower levels were observed in GD patients. Its levels are influenced by age and ERT duration in GD patients, with a negative correlation with age in GD3 patients suggesting a potential disease-related dynamic.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Plasma, Blood samples (in this study); previously reported in erythrocytes.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No statistically significant differences in levels were found between GD patients (median 1.81 ng/mL), GBA1 carriers (median 1.69 ng/mL), and the control group (median 2.08 ng/mL) in this study. However, previous studies reported increased dimerization in erythrocytes of GD patients and a negative correlation between age and protein oligomerization. Correlation with age was also reported in supplementary materials.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Oligomeric forms of alpha-synuclein are associated with neurotoxicity and the progression of synucleinopathies (e.g., Parkinson's disease). Their accumulation and aggregation are linked to dysfunctions of proteolysis machinery, ER stress, and defects of chaperone-mediated autophagy, leading to lysosomal dysfunction.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Gaucher disease (GD) patients, GBA1 variant carriers, healthy controls, aging, and Enzyme Replacement Therapy (ERT) treatment duration.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: An indicator of lysosomal dysfunction and a risk factor for synucleinopathies like Parkinson's disease (PD). In this study, the lack of significant changes in plasma suggests that the disease state or ERT treatment did not lead to detectable alterations in this potentially neurotoxic form.
